read: full: main text pp. 1-10, limitations and appendices A-D.3 (pp. 26-31) read in full; D.4-G (extra results, prompts, failure cases, task examples, task table; pp. 32-61) and the NeurIPS checklist (pp. 18-25) skimmed (section openings and keyword search)
venue_now: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p. 1 footer); the text is arXiv v2, 6 Nov 2025 (p. 1)
what_it_is: EngDesign is a benchmark of 101 open-ended engineering design tasks across nine domains (operating systems, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structures, digital hardware, analog IC, robotics, signal processing), decomposed into 473 gradable rubric items (pp. 2-3; Table 1, p. 5). A model must propose a design (e.g. controller coefficients, a SPICE netlist, a topology-optimisation setting) in a structured output. Task-specific, human-written evaluation scripts check the design through simulation, constraint validation or performance testing (SPICE, MATLAB, structural FEA, MQSim and others) and return pass/fail, a 0-100 partial-credit score and a log (pp. 2, 4-6). Tasks have no unique golden answer; each comes with a validated reference design (p. 5). Twelve model configurations were run three times per task. The best overall pass rate is 34.38% (o3), and every model scores 0% on analog IC design (p. 7).
domain: engineering design: operating systems, computer architecture, control, mechanical systems, structures, digital hardware, analog IC, robotics, signal processing
size: 101 tasks with 473 rubric items (Table 1, p. 5); 67 open tasks (EngDesign-Open) and 34 that need licensed MATLAB or Cadence (p. 3); 23 tasks with image inputs (p. 5); 12 model configurations (4 chat, 8 reasoning, including high-effort o3 and o4-mini), 3 trials per task (p. 7)
source_of_items: expert-written: proposals from graduate students and researchers, drawing on open-source resources and their domain knowledge; 186 proposals from over 40 contributors, 101 accepted (pp. 6, 28); per-task references in Table 15 (pp. 51-61)
has_gold_traces: no: each task has a validated reference design that meets all requirements (p. 5), not a reasoning trace. Models are asked for a step-by-step 'reasoning' field, but only the structured design ('ConfigFile') is parsed and evaluated (pp. 6, 30)
evaluation: simulation-based functional check of the final design by task-specific scripts: binary pass/fail plus a 0-100 rubric score with partial credit, averaged over 3 trials, and 'reasoning robustness' (tasks passed in all trials divided by tasks passed in any trial) (pp. 5-7, 30-31). Not LLM-judged and not step-level; the paper contrasts it with exact string matching or LLM-as-judge scoring (p. 5)
human_validation: Two review rounds (p. 6). In the first, reviewers and the contributor check task clarity, the rubric, that the evaluation code runs and handles edge cases, and that the reference design passes. In the second, faculty experts in the domain check technical soundness. 85 of 186 proposals were discarded (p. 28). No agreement statistics. Failed responses of three models were labelled by hand with five error types (multi-label), with no agreement reported (p. 9).
contamination_measures: none reported; the tasks are newly written by contributors (p. 6), but no contamination analysis or private split is described

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' Also covered by the closing S-E3 (L199-201): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: 'Design generation' is right: models must 'generate functional, objective-oriented engineering designs' (p. 1), such as controllers, circuits and structures (p. 2). 'Tangential' is EngTrace's label, and the paper argues the opposite. It treats design as the core of engineering ('At its core, engineering design is the systematic and creative process...', p. 2) and as harder than textbook problem solving (p. 2). For this paper, S-E3's 'limited to outcome matching' is only half right. EngDesign scores outcomes and never the reasoning (pp. 6, 30), but it does not match answers: there is no unique golden design, and designs are checked by simulation against requirements, with partial credit (p. 5). The paper is cited but not named in the May text.

suggested_wording: EngDesign (Guo et al., 2025b) evaluates open-ended design: for 101 tasks across nine engineering domains, models propose designs that task-specific scripts check against the requirements through simulation (e.g., SPICE, MATLAB) with partial credit, without scoring the reasoning that produced them.
facts_to_cite: 101 design tasks across nine engineering domains, decomposed into 473 gradable rubric items (pp. 2-3; Table 1, p. 5)
Each task has a description, a rubric scored out of 100 with partial credit, an automated evaluation pipeline and a validated reference design (p. 5)

Designs are checked by task-specific, human-written scripts using domain simulators (SPICE, structural finite element analysis, MATLAB Control System Toolbox and others); the pipeline returns pass/fail, a 0-100 score and a log (pp. 2, 5-6)
Tasks have no unique golden design; the paper contrasts its simulation-based checks with exact string matching or LLM-as-judge scoring (p. 5)
Responses include a step-by-step reasoning field, but only the structured design output is parsed for evaluation (pp. 6, 30)
186 task proposals from over 40 contributors went through LLM pre-filtering (o4-mini) and two review rounds, the second by faculty experts; 101 were kept (pp. 6, 28)
No model exceeds a 35% overall pass rate (best: o3, 34.38%), and every model scores 0% on analog IC design (p. 7)
With feedback over ten iterations, o3 reaches almost 60% pass rate on a 71-task subset (p. 9)
In hand-labelled failures of three models, domain-knowledge and constraint-violation errors account for roughly 55-67%; pure computation errors are at most 9% (pp. 9-10)
Published in the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p. 1)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering subject matter (signal processing, structures and mechanical systems overlap in part with EngTrace's electrical (signals and systems), civil (structural analysis) and mechanical branches); expert review of items; a deterministic, non-LLM evaluator; partial credit. Lacks: generated instances (101 static tasks); gold reasoning traces (only a reference design); any step-level or process evaluation (the reasoning field is not scored); contamination measures; validation of the evaluator against expert judgements. Differs in task: open-ended design with many valid answers, against EngTrace's analytical problems with unique computed answers; at least 30 of the 101 tasks (operating systems 8, computer architecture 5, digital hardware 17; Table 1, p. 5) lie outside EngTrace's five branches.
notes: The revised text should name the benchmark (EngDesign). Keep the keys apart: 'Guo et al., 2025a' is DeepSeek-R1 in the May reference list. The author list (p. 1) shares Xingang Guo, Huan Zhang, Lianhui Qin, Yanfeng Ouyang and Bin Hu with TransportBench (Syed et al., 2024; author list per the citation map), which S-E1 cites.
